evidence_quotes.quote: This paper contributes to interdisciplinary understanding of urban water supply by distilling and integrating relevant empirical knowledge on urban dynamics and water issues in SSA, focusing on progress made and associated challenges.

Material for this paper is drawn from the lead authors' research and expert contributions and discussions during a Population-Environment Research Network (PERN) cyberseminar

Since 1990, rural access to drinking water has improved steadily, yet urban access has stagnated or undergone only a marginal increase, including urban coverage with piped water on premises, which accounts for most of the access gained during this period (WHO/UNICEF, 2015b).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban and peri-urban household and community drinking water service access (and briefly sanitation) across sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in informal settlements.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading in substance: Section 4 discusses governance and institutional factors broadly (plain reading) as well as specific rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access in cited studies, including full cost-recovery pricing, invoicing and sanctions for unpaid bills, prepaid water meters, Lifeline tariff blocks, privatization/PPPs, delegated management models (DMM), and Water User Associations (CPPPs) (narrow reading). However, these mechanisms are only summarized narratively from secondary literature rather than empirically tested or systematically synthesized, so the overall study decision remains exclude (E05) under both readings.
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative review / overview article drawn from expert contributions and discussions during a 2015 PERN cyberseminar, supplemented by descriptive UN/DESA urbanization tables and WHO/UNICEF JMP regional coverage tables. It contains no primary empirical data collection or empirical analysis and has no systematic review protocol, search strategy, screening criteria, or systematic empirical synthesis -> exclude under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses outcomes relevant to water access, including access to improved drinking water sources, piped water on premises, intermittency/reliability, affordability, and disconnections, using secondary JMP descriptive tables and narrative citations of prior studies.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is an unsystematic narrative review without a primary empirical study design or systematic synthesis protocol, there is no identifiable study sample or analytical design linking a defined exposure and outcome.

study_design: Narrative literature review / overview article (non-systematic synthesis from an expert cyberseminar)
population_and_sample: Urban, peri-urban, and informal-settlement populations in sub-Saharan Africa (secondary UN/DESA and WHO/UNICEF JMP aggregate regional statistics; no primary sample or systematic review study pool)
exposure: Urban population growth and water governance arrangements discussed narratively (privatization, full cost-recovery tariffs, prepaid meters, Lifeline tariffs, delegated management, and community-public-private partnerships)
outcome: Household and urban drinking water access, piped water on premises, affordability, and reliability (reported as descriptive secondary statistics and narrative summaries of prior literature)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article addresses urban drinking water access in sub-Saharan Africa (c1) and narratively discusses both broad water governance and specific rule-type mechanisms such as cost-recovery tariffs, prepaid meters, Lifeline blocks, and delegated/WUA utility management models (satisfying c2 in topic under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings), it is an unsystematic narrative review/synthesis paper originating from a 2015 PERN cyberseminar. It contains no primary empirical data or methodology and is not a systematic empirical synthesis (no search strategy, eligibility criteria, or structured evidence synthesis), failing Criterion 3 under both the narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings.
